entries.meaning: Janaka worships the lord of Kosala with single-minded reverence as though he were God, joins his palms, humbly praises him, and speaks of his own overflowing fortune. He honours every king and guest with the respect due an equal relation and gives each a fitting seat; one mouth cannot tell the celebration. Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, the guardians of the directions and the sun—knowers of Raghubīra’s power—have assumed noble Brahmin forms to enjoy the spectacle. Janaka, not recognizing them, nevertheless worships them as gods and offers excellent seats.

When the hour comes Vasiṣṭha summons Śatānanda and asks him to bring the princess quickly. The queen rejoices at the priest’s message, gathers wise companions, Brahmin women and clan elders, and performs family rites with auspicious song. The goddesses in women’s guise appear naturally lovely and dark-complexioned; mortal women, unaware who they are, love them more than life and repeatedly honour them as though they were Umā, Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī. They adorn Sītā, arrange the company, and joyfully escort her to the pavilion.

Sītā’s beauty exceeds the reach of a small intellect. As the wedding party sees that wholly pure treasury of loveliness approach, everyone inwardly bows and, looking from her to Rāma, feels every desire fulfilled. Daśaratha and his sons overflow with inexpressible joy; gods bow and rain flowers, sages bless them, and music and celebration immerse men and women in love. Sītā enters the pavilion while royal sages chant benedictions, and the gurus of both families perform every rite proper to the moment.

Sītā’s mother, Janaka’s chief queen, is known to the world; Brahmā seems to have gathered fame, merit, joy and beauty to fashion her. At the proper time sages summon her and married women respectfully lead her in. Sunayanā shines at Janaka’s left like Menā beside Himalaya. King and queen bring golden pitchers and lovely gemmed vessels full of pure fragrant auspicious water, place them before Rāma, and lovingly begin to wash his sacred feet as Vedic blessings sound and flowers fall from heaven.

Prince and princess circle the sacred fire while all respectfully feast their eyes on the indescribable pair. Rāma and Sītā’s reflections sparkle in the jewelled pillars, as though Love and Rati had taken many forms to watch this matchless wedding, appearing and hiding again through longing and modesty. Every observer forgets self, as Janaka has. The delighted sages complete the circuits and all customary gifts; Rāma applies vermilion to Sītā’s head, a beauty like red lotus pollen adorning the moon and drawing a serpent hungry for nectar. Vasiṣṭha then seats bride and groom together.

All the other princes are married with the same rites described for Raghubīra. The dowry is beyond account and fills the golden, jewelled pavilion: blankets, garments, precious fabrics, elephants, chariots, horses, male and female servants, and ornamented cows like wish-fulfilling Surabhis. Even the guardians of the worlds envy what they see. Daśaratha accepts it graciously and distributes to petitioners whatever each desires; the remainder goes to the guests’ lodging. Janaka then joins his hands and gently addresses the honoured wedding party.

Rāma’s naturally lovely dark body shames millions of Loves. Red-dyed lotus feet shelter the bee-like minds of sages; a pure yellow dhoti eclipses the radiance of lightning in the young sun. A tinkling girdle and sacred thread adorn his waist, ornaments his broad arms, and a ring steals the heart. Wedding jewels cover his broad chest; a yellow upper cloth crosses beneath his arm and gemmed pearls hang from both ends. Lotus eyes, elegant earrings, a perfect face, brows, nose and forehead-mark culminate in a lovely crown woven with auspicious pearls and gems.

entries.meaning: Janaka next invites the wedding party to a grand feast. Matchless cloths are laid as pathways and Daśaratha comes with his sons. The host respectfully washes everyone’s feet and seats each according to rank; his humility and affection as he washes Daśaratha’s feet defy description. He washes Rāma’s lotus feet, hidden in Śiva’s heart, then those of all three brothers, regarding them as Rāma’s equals. Cooks and servers are summoned; leaf plates and gem-set golden betel trays are arranged, and courteous cooks quickly serve fragrant rice, clarified butter and pure, delicious dishes.

After offering the customary first five morsels, the guests begin eating and delight in affectionate wedding taunts sung around them. Countless nectar-like preparations arrive; skilful servers present varieties and flavours too numerous even to name. Men and women weave each diner’s name into sweet comic verses suited to the occasion, and Daśaratha laughs with the whole company. When all have eaten, they receive water for rinsing and betel; Janaka honours Daśaratha and the assembly, and the crowned kings return happily to their lodging.

Fresh celebrations arise each day in the city, making days and nights pass like instants. At dawn Daśaratha awakens to petitioners singing his virtues, gazes upon his four sons with their excellent brides, completes his morning duties, and approaches the guru overflowing with love. He tells Vasiṣṭha that by the sage’s grace his purpose is fulfilled and asks him to summon Brahmins so he may give them beautifully adorned cows. Vāmadeva, Nārada, Vālmīki, Jābāli, Kauśika and many other ascetics assemble.
